starter: Bismillah. Write one sentence about a time something unexpected changed your plans.
What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
Name three things a person needs to survive.
What do you already know about the Amazon rainforest?

teach.heading: Retrieval and inference
bullets: Retrieval: the text tells you directly
Inference: you read between the lines
Both need evidence from the text
teach.note: Read Chapters 1–2 aloud from the class copy (pupils follow in theirs). Pause after the crash and ask for one fact and one inference. Misconception: pupils treat any sentence about the book as an inference; push for 'which words make you think that?'

left.title: Retrieval
points: The answer is on the page

right.title: Inference
points: What sort of person is he?

teach.heading: How openings hook us
bullets: Start in the middle of the action
Create questions in the reader's mind
Give us someone to care about
teach.note: Ask: 'What questions does the opening make you ask?' Collect three in the chat. Link to the big question: one event (the crash) changes everything.

teach.heading: Practise on a short extract
teach.note: Use this original extract to model, so we are not quoting the novel. Ask: what can we retrieve? What can we infer about the speaker?

quote.text: The engine coughed twice, then fell silent. Through the window, the green went on forever, and Sami realised he could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind.

teach.heading: Writing an inference
teach.note: Model on the shared screen.

model.problem: What can we infer about Sami from the extract?
steps: Point: Sami is terrified
Evidence: he 'could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind'
Explain: the noise overwhelms him, suggesting panic and danger
model.answer: A short inference paragraph using evidence

teach.heading: Check: retrieve or infer?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: 'The engine coughed twice, then fell silent.' Which is an INFERENCE?
check.why: The danger is suggested, not stated. A, B and D are stated or retrieved.

practice: Retrieve two facts about the plane journey from Chapter 1.
Write one inference about Fred with a piece of evidence.
List two questions the opening makes you ask.
independent: Core: Write a PEE paragraph: What is your first impression of Fred?
Extend: Explain how the writer hooks the reader in the opening, using two pieces of evidence.
Stretch: Predict how Fred might change by the end of the novel. Justify your prediction with clues from Chapters 1–2.
exit: What is the difference between retrieval and inference?
Write one inference about the setting.
Make one prediction with a reason.
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 3–4 and record two facts and two inferences in your reading journal.
lessons.send: Support: sentence starters ('I can infer that… because…') and the audio version of the chapters. EAL: key word cards. Stretch: compare with another survival story you know.

teach.heading: VANCAPPI: our word-class toolkit
teach.note: Display the school's VANCAPPI poster. Pupils hold up one example for each on the mini-whiteboard.

teach.heading: Sentence boundaries
teach.note: Two complete sentences need a full stop, a semi-colon or a conjunction between them, never just a comma.

misconception.wrong: The plane fell, the children screamed.
misconception.right: The plane fell. The children screamed. / The plane fell and the children screamed.

teach.heading: Model: fix and upgrade
teach.note: Think aloud through the steps.

model.problem: Fix: 'Con was scared she walked slowly through the trees'
steps: Find the two main clauses: Con was scared | she walked slowly...
Choose a boundary: full stop or conjunction
Upgrade the verb: walked becomes edged
Check: capital letter and full stop
model.answer: Con was scared, so she edged slowly through the trees.

teach.heading: Hinge: which is correct?
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: The river was fast, Max held on.
The river was fast. Max held on.
The river was fast Max held on.
check.why: Only B separates the two main clauses; A is a comma splice and C is a run-on sentence.

practice.q: Label every word in: 'Suddenly, the small boat drifted beneath the dark trees.'
practice.a: Suddenly (adverb), the (determiner), small (adjective), boat (noun), drifted (verb), beneath (preposition), the (determiner), dark (adjective), trees (noun).
practice.model: Work left to right: ask 'what job does this word do?' Suddenly tells when (adverb). Small describes boat (adjective). Boat is a thing (noun). Drifted is the action (verb). Beneath shows position (preposition). Note 'the' is a determiner, a word class beyond VANCAPPI.

practice.q: Fix the comma splice: 'Lila found water, she shared it with everyone.'
practice.a: Lila found water. She shared it with everyone. (or: Lila found water and she shared it with everyone.)

independent.q: Core: correct the five sentence-boundary errors in the paragraph on the pupil PDF.
independent.a: Each comma splice or run-on is split with a full stop or joined with a conjunction (and, but, so, because).
independent.model: First error: 'The rain stopped, the forest steamed.' Two main clauses, so: 'The rain stopped. The forest steamed.' or 'The rain stopped and the forest steamed.'

independent.q: Extend: write three sentences about surviving in the rainforest, each using a different conjunction.
independent.a: For example: Fred climbed the tree because he wanted to see the river.

independent.q: Stretch: write one sentence containing all eight VANCAPPI word classes.
independent.a: For example: 'Oh, she quickly ran under the bridge and hid.' (interjection Oh, pronoun she, adverb quickly, verb ran, preposition under, noun bridge, conjunction and, verb hid; add an adjective: 'the old bridge').

exit.q: Which word class is 'although'? A) adverb B) conjunction C) preposition
exit.a: B) conjunction

exit.q: Write the shortest sentence you can with a verb, a noun and an interjection.
exit.a: For example: 'Oh! Birds sang.'

lessons.homework: Grammar Booklet: VANCAPPI and sentence boundaries exercises; learn the eight word classes in order.
lessons.send: SEND: VANCAPPI card with colour-coded examples. EAL: bilingual word-class glossary. Stretch: identify determiners and modal verbs as well.

lessons.title: Bridge: how writers build a setting (The Explorer essentials)
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer make a place feel dangerous?
objectives: To understand how writers choose words to make a setting feel alive and dangerous
successCriteria: All: find three precise words that build the rainforest setting
Most: explain what one word suggests about the place
Some: explain how the setting reflects a character's feelings
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Amazon rainforest's layers (canopy, understorey, forest floor)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the variety of the natural world

keywords.def: where and when a story takes place
the mood or feeling a place gives the reader
working out what is suggested, not stated

hook.text: Imagine waking up alone in a rainforest. What is the first thing you would hear, and how would it make you feel?

pictures.alt: The Amazon rainforest canopy from above
Tangled roots on a rainforest floor
A river winding through the Amazon

resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary English scheme of work 2026-27, Year 7 HT1 weekly scheme (The Explorer: setting and language analysis)
Teacher-written rainforest setting extract (on the slides and pupil PDF)
Reading Journal (school template)
Pupil PDF worksheet (printable or for a drawing tablet)

starter.q: Which word is a noun? A) canopy B) dripping C) slowly
Which sentence uses a full stop correctly? A) The river was wide. It was brown. B) The river was wide it was brown.
options: The river was wide. It was brown.
The river was wide it was brown.
starter.a: A) The river was wide. It was brown.

starter.q: What is an inference? A) a fact copied from the text B) an idea worked out from clues C) a summary
options: a fact copied from the text
an idea worked out from clues
starter.a: B) an idea worked out from clues

teach.heading: The Explorer: what we need to know
bullets: Four children survive a plane crash in the Amazon.
The rainforest is both beautiful and deadly.
The novel asks: how do people change through hardship?
teach.note: Introduce Katherine Rundell's novel (2017) as the school's Year 7 Autumn text. Pupils will read it in full in Autumn 2027; today we learn the skill of reading a setting. Show the map picture and ask what pupils already know about the Amazon.

teach.heading: Words that build a setting
bullets: Adjectives that carry mood: humid, tangled, silent
teach.note: Use this teacher-written line: 'The trees swallowed the light, and the air hung heavy and wet.' Ask which word does the most work. Draw out 'swallowed' (personification: the forest seems alive and hungry).

quote.text: The trees swallowed the light, and the air hung heavy and wet. Somewhere above, something shrieked and fell silent.

teach.heading: Model: from word to effect
teach.note: Think aloud. Show how one word leads to an inference about the place and the character.

model.problem: What does 'swallowed' suggest about the rainforest?
steps: Find the word: swallowed
Literal meaning: eaten whole
Connotation: hunger, danger, being trapped
Inference: the forest feels alive and threatening
model.answer: The verb 'swallowed' makes the forest seem like a hungry creature, so the reader senses danger.

teach.heading: Hinge: which word builds tension?
teach.note: Poll. Reveal the answer and discuss why the others are weaker.

check.q: Which word makes the setting most threatening?
check.why: 'Shrieked' is a sudden, frightening sound; 'green' and 'trees' are neutral, 'wet' is uncomfortable but not threatening.

practice.q: Explain what 'hung heavy' suggests about the air.
practice.a: It suggests the air is thick, humid and hard to breathe, creating an oppressive mood.
practice.model: Word: hung heavy. Meaning: the air feels weighed down. Connotation: pressure, discomfort. Inference: the heat is oppressive and the place feels hostile.

practice.q: Find a word in the extract that shows sound and explain its effect.
practice.a: 'Shrieked': a sudden scream that breaks the silence and makes the reader jump.

independent.q: Core: write three sentences explaining how the extract makes the rainforest feel dangerous. Use 'This suggests...' in each.
independent.a: For example: The verb 'swallowed' suggests the forest is alive and hungry. This suggests the children could be trapped...
independent.model: The verb 'swallowed' suggests the trees are like a hungry animal. This suggests the rainforest could trap anyone inside it. The reader feels uneasy because the place itself seems alive.

independent.q: Extend: add a sentence about how a lost child might feel in this setting.
independent.a: For example: A lost child would feel small and watched, because the forest seems to have a will of its own.

independent.q: Stretch: write your own sentence about the rainforest using one verb that makes it seem alive.
independent.a: For example: Vines coiled around the trunks like patient snakes.

exit.q: Which is the best explanation? A) 'Swallowed' is a good word B) 'Swallowed' makes the forest seem hungry and alive
options: 'Swallowed' makes the forest seem hungry and alive
exit.a: B) 'Swallowed' makes the forest seem hungry and alive

exit.q: Return to the ponder question: which word from today would you use to describe that first sound, and why?
exit.a: Answers vary, e.g. 'shrieked', because it is sudden and frightening.

lessons.homework: Read the setting extract on the pupil PDF again and underline five words that build atmosphere; start your Reading Journal with the date and one new word.
lessons.send: SEND: word bank with meanings and a 'This suggests...' sentence starter. EAL: picture glossary of rainforest nouns. Stretch: comment on how two words work together.

starter.q: Which is a subordinating conjunction? A) although B) and C) but
Where does the comma go? 'When night fell the house creaked.' A) after 'fell' B) after 'house'
What does PETZAAL's E stand for? A) Effect B) Evidence C) Explain

teach.heading: STASS: the school's setting framework
teach.note: Go through each letter with an example from the old house.

head: Step
Ask
Example
rows: Bruised clouds pressed down on the roof.
It was the hour after sunset.
The silence felt like held breath.
From the gate, up the path, to the door.

teach.heading: Model: a STASS paragraph
teach.note: Read the model and label each step together.

model.problem: Describe an old house at dusk
steps: Sky: Bruised clouds pressed down on the slate roof.
Time: It was the hour when shadows grow long.
Atmosphere: As I stepped closer, the silence felt like held breath.
Significant object: Inside, a clock had stopped at 3:17.
Spatial order: From the gate to the door, weeds swallowed the path.
model.answer: A paragraph where the weather, time and objects build one mood.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: 'Rain wept against the window as she waited alone.' This is...
check.why: The weather (weeping rain) mirrors a sad, lonely feeling: pathetic fallacy.

practice.q: Plan your STASS grid for 'a corridor in an old school at night'.
practice.a: Five notes, one per STASS step.
practice.model: Sky: wind moaning at the windows. Time: midnight. Atmosphere: watchful, still. Significant object: a single locker door swinging. Spatial order: from the stairs, along the corridor, to the last classroom.

practice.q: Write your Sky sentence using pathetic fallacy.
practice.a: For example: Outside, the wind moaned as if it had lost something.

independent.q: Core: write your STASS setting paragraph in the portal response box (at least six sentences, one complex sentence). Starter: 'Outside, the wind...'
independent.a: A paragraph using all five STASS steps, a complex sentence and precise verbs.
independent.model: Outside, the wind moaned against the tall windows. It was midnight, and the school had forgotten its daytime noise. As I walked along the corridor, my footsteps sounded too loud. Halfway down, a single locker door swung open and shut. At the far end, the last classroom glowed with a pale light that should not have been there.

independent.q: DIRT: use the feedback code to improve two sentences in green pen.
independent.a: Two sentences improved (verb, boundary or clause).

independent.q: Stretch: change the mood of one sentence from creepy to peaceful by changing only two words.
independent.a: For example: 'the wind moaned' becomes 'the wind whispered'; 'should not' becomes 'seemed to'.

exit.q: What does the first S in STASS stand for? A) Sound B) Sky C) Shape
exit.a: B) Sky

exit.q: Return to the ponder: which words changed the mood most, and why?
exit.a: Usually the verbs and the weather, because they carry feelings.

lessons.homework: Write a STASS paragraph about your street at dawn; label each step.
lessons.send: SEND: STASS planning grid with word bank. EAL: model paragraph to adapt by changing nouns. Stretch: use pathetic fallacy and a relative clause.

keywords.def: how a writer presents a character
the words characters speak
a quality of a person's character
explain similarities and differences

starter: Name the four children in The Explorer.
Give one quality of a good leader.

teach.heading: How writers reveal character
teach.note: Use Chapters 7–10 from the class copy. Pupils find one example of each for Fred or Con.

teach.heading: Comparing leaders

teach.note: Common error.

check.q: 'She handed the last biscuit to the youngest without a word.' What does this action suggest?
check.why: Giving away scarce food silently shows quiet generosity. The action reveals character.

Decide: who is the best leader so far? One reason.

find and take information from a text
the first sentence of a paragraph, saying what it is about
give the main points briefly

starter.q: Which word is a verb? A) river B) flows C) muddy
Fiction or non-fiction: an encyclopedia entry about frogs? A) fiction B) non-fiction

teach.heading: Features of an information text
teach.note: Show the teacher-written text on the pupil PDF: 'The Amazon Rainforest'. Ask pupils to spot each feature before you name it.

teach.heading: The rainforest in layers
teach.note: Teach the four layers from the diagram picture; this is the information pupils will retrieve.

items: Forest floor: roots and fallen leaves

teach.heading: Model: retrieve, then summarise
teach.note: Show how to find facts quickly by scanning for key words, then squeeze a paragraph into one sentence.

model.problem: Summarise the paragraph on the canopy.
steps: Scan for the heading 'The canopy'
Underline the topic sentence
Pick two key facts
Write one sentence in your own words
model.answer: The canopy is a thick roof of leaves where most rainforest animals live.

teach.heading: Hinge: what is a topic sentence for?
teach.note: Poll, then discuss.

check.q: A topic sentence...
options: tells the reader what the paragraph is about
check.why: It introduces the paragraph's main idea; it is not the end, and it is rarely a question.

practice.q: Retrieve two facts about the forest floor from the text.
practice.a: It is dark because little sunlight reaches it; it is covered in roots and fallen leaves.
practice.model: Scan for 'forest floor'. Read the topic sentence. Copy the two facts in short phrases: dark, little sunlight; roots and fallen leaves.

practice.q: Which heading would you look under to find out about jaguars?
practice.a: The understorey or forest floor section, where large animals hunt.

independent.q: Core: answer the four retrieval questions on the pupil PDF in full sentences.
independent.a: Answers from the teacher-written text: the four layers, the canopy roof, the dark understorey, the forest floor's roots and leaves.
independent.model: Question: Why is the understorey dark? Answer in a full sentence using the question's words: The understorey is dark because the canopy above blocks most of the sunlight.

independent.q: Extend: summarise the whole text in two sentences.
independent.a: For example: The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest, arranged in layers from the emergent trees to the forest floor. Each layer has its own conditions and wildlife.

independent.q: Stretch: how would Fred, Con, Lila and Max use this information to survive? Give one idea.
independent.a: For example: they could look for food and water near the river, because the forest floor is dark and hard to search.

exit.q: Which is a summary? A) a long retelling B) the main points briefly C) a list of every fact
exit.a: B) the main points briefly

exit.q: Is 'the lungs of the Earth' a fair name? Give one reason from today.
exit.a: Answers vary, e.g. yes, because its vast canopy of trees takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen.

lessons.homework: Find one fact about an Amazon animal and write it as a topic sentence plus two supporting facts.
lessons.send: SEND: retrieval questions with paragraph numbers. EAL: key word glossary with pictures. Stretch: explain why the text uses the third person.

Often a choice or a discovery

teach.heading: Sentence length and tension

quote.text: They crept along the ledge, fingers clutching wet stone, the river roaring somewhere far below them in the dark, and every step felt like a question nobody wanted to answer. Then the rock gave way.

model.problem: How does the writer build tension in the extract?

We feel the characters' careful, fearful movement

It shocks the reader, like the fall itself

teach.note: Link to the big question.

teach.note: Show me on 3.

options: To create a sudden shock or change of pace
check.why: Contrast in sentence length changes pace and creates impact.

practice: Identify a turning point and explain what changes.
Find a short sentence in the novel and explain its effect.
Describe how one character has changed since Chapter 1.

teach.heading: Active voice
teach.note: Label S, V, O on the slide.

model.problem: Make passive: 'The police arrested Stanley.'
steps: Find the object: Stanley
Move it to the front: Stanley...
Add was + past participle: was arrested
Optional agent: by the police
model.answer: Stanley was arrested (by the police). Without the agent, the reader focuses on what happened to Stanley.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which sentence is passive?
check.why: 'Were given' is was/were + past participle with the object at the front; the others are active.

practice.q: Make passive: 'The boys dug fifty holes.'
practice.a: Fifty holes were dug (by the boys).
practice.model: Object: fifty holes. Front it: 'Fifty holes...'. Verb: were + dug. Agent optional: by the boys. Answer: Fifty holes were dug by the boys.

practice.q: Make active: 'The shoes were stolen by a thief.'
practice.a: A thief stole the shoes.

independent.q: Core: rewrite the account of Stanley's arrest on the pupil PDF twice: once all active, once with three passive sentences.
independent.a: Two accurate versions; passive sentences use was/were + past participle.
independent.model: Active: 'A police officer stopped Stanley.' Passive: 'Stanley was stopped.' Notice the passive hides who stopped him, which makes Stanley seem powerless.

independent.q: Extend: which version is more effective at showing Stanley's helplessness? Explain in two sentences.
independent.a: The passive, because things happen to Stanley and the people in power are hidden.

independent.q: Stretch: find or write a sentence where the passive is used to avoid blame.
independent.a: For example: 'Mistakes were made.' The speaker hides who made them.

exit.q: 'The hole was dug.' Is this A) active B) passive?
exit.a: B) passive

exit.q: Return to the ponder: why might someone say 'Mistakes were made'?
exit.a: To avoid saying who made them and so avoid blame.

teach.heading: Power at Camp Green Lake
teach.note: Use the character relationship map from the knowledge organiser.

items: Mr Sir: threats and harsh rules

teach.heading: How Sachar shows misused authority
teach.note: Pupils will have read chapters 11 to 17 at home. Draw out that the digging is not about 'building character' but searching for something the Warden wants.

teach.heading: Model: PETZAAL on authority
teach.note: Go through the labelled model.

model.problem: How does Sachar present authority through the adults?
steps: Point: Sachar presents the adults as using power for themselves.
Evidence: the Warden makes the boys dig where Stanley's find was made (chapters 11 to 17).
Zoom in: the digging becomes a search, not a lesson.
Alternative: Mr Pendanski seems kind, but his kindness hides contempt.
Link: so authority at the camp is self-serving and unjust.
model.answer: A PETZAAL paragraph on self-serving authority.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Why does the Warden really make the boys dig?
options: to search for something she wants
check.why: The 'character' reason is a cover; the hidden purpose is the search. This is the key to the misuse of authority.

practice.q: Which adult uses fear most? Give one example.
practice.a: Mr Sir: he uses threats and harsh rules (for example over water).
practice.model: Choose Mr Sir. Example: he controls the water the boys need in the heat. Effect: the boys must obey to survive, so his power rests on fear.

practice.q: How does Stanley's place in the hierarchy change in these chapters?
practice.a: He begins to be accepted by the group but is still used by X-Ray.

independent.q: Core: write a PETZAAL paragraph in the portal response box: 'How does Sachar present authority through the adults at Camp Green Lake?' Starter: 'Sachar presents the adults at Camp Green Lake as...'
independent.a: A PETZAAL paragraph with a short quotation from the class copy and an alternative reading.
independent.model: Point: Sachar presents the adults as using their authority for their own gain. | Evidence: the boys are told digging will build character (find the line in chapters 11 to 17) | Technique: dramatic irony | Zoom in: 'character' is a noble word used to hide a selfish search. | Analyse: The reader sees that the adults lie, so their authority loses all respect. | Alternative: Some readers may see Mr Sir as following orders, less guilty than the Warden. | Link: So Sachar presents authority at the camp as dishonest and unjust.

independent.q: Extend: compare two adults: who is more dangerous, Mr Sir or Mr Pendanski? Why?
independent.a: Answers vary, e.g. Mr Pendanski, because his cruelty is hidden behind friendliness.

independent.q: Stretch: how is X-Ray's power over the boys like the adults' power?
independent.a: He also uses his position for himself, taking credit for others' finds.

exit.q: Mr Pendanski's kindness is... A) genuine B) a mask for contempt
exit.a: B) a mask for contempt

exit.q: Return to the ponder: which adult at camp is obeyed, and is anyone trusted?
exit.a: The Warden is obeyed through fear; none of the adults is truly trusted.

lessons.send: SEND: character cards with key events; PETZAAL frame. EAL: authority word bank. Stretch: link to the idea that leadership is a trust (amanah).

model.problem: Opening paragraph about a water shortage at camp
steps: Who: boys at Camp Green Lake
What: water ran short during digging
Where: Camp Green Lake, Texas
When: on Tuesday afternoon
Why: a delivery was late (according to staff)
model.answer: Boys at Camp Green Lake, Texas, were left without water on Tuesday afternoon after a delivery was late, according to staff.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which is an opinion?
options: 'It is a wonderful place for boys,' said the Warden.
check.why: The Warden's claim cannot be proved; it is her view, which the reporter has chosen to include.

practice.q: Sort the six statements on the pupil PDF into fact and opinion.
practice.a: Facts: location, date, temperature; Opinions: 'wonderful', 'lazy boys', 'deserved'.
practice.model: Ask of each: could I prove it? 'The camp is in Texas' can be checked on a map, so fact. 'The boys are lazy' is a judgement, so opinion.

practice.q: Whose voice is missing from the teacher-written report, and what effect does that have?
practice.a: Stanley's (and the boys'); the report favours the adults' view.

independent.q: Core: write a newspaper report in the portal response box about an incident at Camp Green Lake: headline, 5 Ws opening, two eyewitness quotations, third person. Starter: headline then 'Boys at Camp Green Lake...'
independent.a: A report with all features and a balance of voices.
independent.model: HEADLINE: Water Runs Dry at Desert Camp. Boys at Camp Green Lake, Texas, were left without water on Tuesday afternoon after a delivery was late. 'We were digging for hours,' said one camper. A member of staff said the problem was 'quickly solved'. The camp is now under review.

independent.q: Extend: rewrite one sentence to show bias for the boys, then for the staff.
independent.a: For example: 'Desperate boys begged for water' vs 'Staff swiftly restored supplies'.

independent.q: Stretch: explain how the choice of quotations can create bias.
independent.a: Choosing only one side's voice makes readers trust that side.

exit.q: The first paragraph of a report usually answers... A) the 5 Ws B) a riddle
exit.a: A) the 5 Ws

exit.q: Return to the ponder: how can two true reports give different impressions?
exit.a: By choosing different facts, quotations and words.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

He digs until he was exhausted.

practice.q: Name the tense: 'Zero had never been to school.'
practice.a: Past perfect.

practice.q: Correct the tense error: 'Stanley walks to the hole and found a tube.'

independent.q: Core: rewrite the teacher-written Holes-style scene on the pupil PDF in the present tense, keeping the tense consistent.

independent.q: Extend: evaluate: which version is more effective and why? Two sentences.
independent.a: The present feels more immediate and tense; the past feels like a story being told.

independent.q: Stretch: add one sentence in the past perfect to create a flashback.

exit.q: Return to the ponder: which version felt more urgent and why?

model.problem: How does Sachar present justice and redemption through Stanley's journey?
steps: Point: Stanley is redeemed by choosing loyalty over self-interest.
Evidence 1: early on he accepts the blame for others to survive.
Evidence 2: later he carries Zero up the mountain (class copy).
Analyse: his strength grows with his kindness.
Alternative: some see the ending as luck, not justice.

model.answer: A whole-text PETZAAL paragraph tracing change.

teach.note: Poll.

check.q: What does the return of rain at the end suggest?
check.why: Rain after a long drought symbolises renewal and justice restored; it links back to 'There is no lake'.

practice.q: Give one piece of evidence that Stanley has changed by the end.
practice.a: He risks his life to help Zero, showing courage and loyalty.
practice.model: Start: Stanley thinks he is a victim of bad luck. Evidence of change: he chooses to help Zero though it is dangerous. So he has become active and brave.

practice.q: How does the ending answer the opening line?
practice.a: The lake starts to return, reversing 'There is no lake at Camp Green Lake.'

independent.q: Core: write an extended PETZAAL response in the portal response box (two paragraphs): 'How does Sachar present justice and redemption through Stanley's journey?' Starter: 'At the start of the novel, Stanley...'
independent.a: Two PETZAAL paragraphs using evidence from the beginning and the end.
independent.model: Point: At the start of the novel, Stanley is a passive victim, but by the end he has earned redemption through loyalty. | Evidence: There is no lake at Camp Green Lake (opening) and the rain at the end | Technique: symbolism and cyclical structure | Zoom in: 'no lake' becomes rain: emptiness turns to renewal. | Analyse: The change in the land mirrors Stanley's inner change, suggesting justice is finally done. | Alternative: Some readers think the happy ending is too neat, relying on luck. | Link: So Sachar presents redemption as earned by kindness and courage, not handed out by fate.

independent.q: Extend: add a sentence on Zero's transformation.

model.problem: Should children be punished like adults?
steps: Point: Children should not be punished exactly like adults.
Evidence: the article says young people's judgement is still developing.
Explain: they can change more easily, so help is more effective than harsh punishment.
Develop: some argue victims deserve equal justice; however, protecting the public is better achieved by real change.
Link: so fairness means consequences that fit a child's stage of life.
model.answer: A balanced PEEDL paragraph.

teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which sentence develops a counter-argument?
options: Some argue that harsh punishment deters crime; however, evidence suggests support reduces reoffending more.
check.why: B states the other side, then answers it with evidence.

practice.q: Give one argument for and one against from the article.
practice.a: For: deterrence protects victims. Against: children are still developing and respond to rehabilitation.
practice.model: Scan for 'on the other hand'. The article's first side is deterrence; its second side is rehabilitation. Write each in one sentence.

practice.q: How does Camp Green Lake fail as a place of rehabilitation?
practice.a: It punishes and exploits the boys instead of helping them change.

independent.q: Core: write a balanced PEEDL response in the portal response box: 'Should children be punished like adults?' Starter: 'Although some people believe..., I believe...'
independent.a: One or two PEEDL paragraphs with evidence, a counter-argument and a clear judgement.
independent.model: Point: Children should face consequences, but not exactly the same as adults. | Evidence: The article explains that young people's judgement is still developing. | Explain: This means they are more able to change, so support works better than harsh punishment. | Develop: Although some argue victims deserve equal justice, Camp Green Lake shows that punishment without help only causes more harm. | Link: Therefore, fair justice for children should aim to change them, not just to make them suffer.

independent.q: Extend: use one example from Holes as evidence.
independent.a: For example: the boys at Camp Green Lake are made worse, not better, by pointless punishment.

independent.q: Stretch: add a one-sentence conclusion that weighs both sides.
independent.a: For example: 'Justice for children must protect the public and give a real chance to change.'

exit.q: In PEEDL, the D is where we... A) develop with a counter-argument B) describe the setting
exit.a: A) develop with a counter-argument

exit.q: Return to the ponder: what would be fair for the 12-year-old?
exit.a: Answers vary; strong answers mention consequences that fit age and a chance to change.

model.problem: Improve: 'Stanley is weak. Stanley helps Zero. Stanley is brave.'
steps: Topic sentence: Across the novel, Stanley grows in courage.
Sequence: At first, he accepts whatever happens to him.
Contrast: However, by the end he chooses to risk his life for Zero.
Refer back: This choice shows...
model.answer: Across the novel, Stanley grows in courage. At first, he accepts whatever happens to him; however, by the end he risks his life for Zero. This choice shows how friendship has transformed him.

check.q: Which word best links two contrasting ideas?
check.why: 'However' signals contrast; the others add or sequence.

practice.q: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about Zero's change.
practice.a: For example: 'Sachar presents Zero as a character who is underestimated but grows in confidence.'
practice.model: Ask: what is the paragraph about, and what is my argument? Character: Zero. Argument: he is underestimated but grows. Combine: 'Sachar presents Zero as underestimated, yet he grows in confidence.'

practice.q: Join with a cohesive device: 'Zero is silent. Zero learns to read.'
practice.a: At first, Zero is silent; however, once he learns to read, he finds his voice.

independent.q: Core: plan and write a complete whole-text PETZAAL response in the portal response box (three paragraphs, each with a topic sentence and a discourse marker): 'How does Sachar present Stanley's transformation?' Starter: 'Across the novel, Sachar...'
independent.a: Three cohesive paragraphs (start, camp, end) with topic sentences and markers.
independent.model: Across the novel, Sachar presents Stanley's transformation from victim to hero. At first, Stanley blames his bad luck... Later, at the camp, friendship with Zero begins to change him... Ultimately, by the end, his loyalty is rewarded and the past is put right.

independent.q: Extend: underline every cohesive device you used.
independent.a: At least five devices underlined.

independent.q: Stretch: write a conclusion that does not just repeat the paragraphs.
independent.a: A conclusion that states the writer's message about justice.

exit.q: A topic sentence comes... A) at the start of a paragraph B) at the end

exit.a: A) at the start of a paragraph

exit.q: Answer the ponder: what are the 'joining pieces' of an essay?
exit.a: Topic sentences and cohesive devices such as however, furthermore, at first, ultimately.
